name: Bonepulling

card.summary: A manual practice of applying sustained force to the palate or facial bones, promoted online as a way to reshape the midface and jaw toward a more forward, defined look.
card.aka: bone pulling, thumbpulling, progressive stress exercises
card.note: Force applied to teeth, jaw joints and the neck can cause injury; orthodontists describe supervised appliances, not hand pulling, as the method for moving facial structures.

quick.overview:
Bonepulling is a do-it-yourself practice in which a person uses their hands, usually the thumbs, to apply steady force to part of the face, most often the palate, in the hope of nudging the upper jaw forward or wider. Followers aim for a more projected midface, broader palate and stronger facial structure.

Proponents compare it to orthodontic appliances, which also apply slow, constant force, and argue that bone adapts to loading. Orthodontists and craniofacial specialists describe appliances and surgery, supervised by clinicians, as the established routes to moving facial bones, and no published trial has tested manual bonepulling.
quick.how: Guides circulating on looksmax.org describe bonepulling as a series of sessions using thumb pressure on the soft palate, with variations in direction (forward, lateral and reverse) and cushioning or head support to spread the force. Followers describe it as a long-term routine, usually combined with tongue-posture practices such as mewing.
quick.risks: Risks that clinicians associate with unsupervised force on the mouth and face include tooth loosening or movement, gum and palate injury, jaw-joint strain and neck strain. Guides themselves warn against pushing on teeth and recommend head support. No published trial shows that hand pulling changes adult facial bones.

lead: Bonepulling (also written bone pulling, and related to thumbpulling and progressive-stress exercises) is a practice in looksmaxxing communities in which a person applies sustained manual force to facial structures, most commonly the palate, to try to change facial bone position. The goal is a more forward, wider or more projected midface and jaw.[1][2]

Its rationale, as laid out in a multi-part guide series on looksmax.org, rests on mechanotransduction: the idea that bone and muscle adapt to mechanical stress, as seen with orthodontic appliances that apply slow, steady force.[2] Proponents argue that hand-applied force could work in a similar way.

Orthodontists move teeth and jaws with clinician-supervised appliances and surgery, and no published human study has tested manual bonepulling. Related claims about tongue posture (mewing) are described by Wikipedia as unproven, with experts quoted as saying no credible research has shown the approach changes jaw structure.[3]

chain: Apply sustained force to the palate or facial bones
Claimed adaptation of the bone to the stress
angle.text: Followers use bonepulling to try to move the upper jaw forward or expand the palate, aiming for a more projected midface. They frame it as the DIY counterpart of orthodontic appliances, which also work by steady force.

paras: Bonepulling guides describe pulling or pushing against the palate with the thumbs, with the stated aim of encouraging palate expansion and forward growth of the maxilla.[1] One guide specifies pulling against the soft palate at the back of the mouth rather than against the teeth, and says teeth move as a consequence of palate expansion.[1] It also advises cushioning for the thumbs and leaning the head on a wall or shelf so that neck and spine do not bear the force.[1] Variants named in the series include forward, lateral and reverse directions.[1]

The opening guide in the series argues that orthodontic appliances produce change through slow, consistent, progressive stress, and that bone, muscle and fat adapt to force via mechanotransduction, in which osteocytes sense strain and trigger remodelling.[2] Followers apply this to manual force, describing it as a no-cost counterpart to braces and palatal expanders.[2]
Forum members also discuss related ideas, such as using belts or straps to try to move parts of the midface back, which other members in the thread treated as speculative.[4]

Published literature on bone anchors and orthopaedic fixation concerns surgical hardware and does not address manual facial force.[5] Orthodontists use controlled appliances placed and monitored by clinicians, and craniofacial surgeons use procedures such as Le Fort osteotomies to reposition the midface.[4] The wider oral-posture movement is described on Wikipedia as an unproven form of training, with a 2019 paper in the Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery quoted as saying no credible research has proven orthotropics effective.[3]

The guides themselves note risks that they try to manage, such as protecting thumbs, avoiding force on teeth and supporting the head to spare neck ligaments.[1] Dental professionals generally associate uncontrolled force on teeth with movement, loosening and gum injury, and jaw-joint strain is a recognised concern with repeated loading.

lore.intro: Bonepulling is discussed on looksmax.org in a multi-part guide series on progressive stress, alongside other bonehack practices.[2]

claims.claim: Sustained hand pressure on the palate can expand the palate and move the maxilla forward
claims.believers: Guide authors compare it to orthodontic force and cite mechanotransduction, saying bone adapts to slow progressive stress.[1][2]
claims.experts: No published study has tested manual bonepulling; orthodontic movement is described in the clinical literature using supervised appliances.[3]

claims.claim: Strap or belt pressure could move an overprojected midface backward
claims.believers: A forum poster proposed wrapping a belt around the midface, while rating the odds as low.[4]
claims.experts: Surgical repositioning of the midface is done with osteotomies by surgeons, not external straps.[4]
